text:
[curious] But what's the standard error of a median? Or a correlation? The formula is ugly, or doesn't exist. The bootstrap's answer is bold: treat your sample as if it were the population. Here are sixty customer wait times, skewed, not normal. Draw sixty from them, with replacement. Some come up twice, or three times... and some not at all. Average that resample. Then do it all again, five thousand times. The averages pile up into a bootstrap distribution. Its spread is the standard error, zero point four eight, where the formula says zero point four nine. And its middle ninety-five percent, six point one to eight point oh, is almost exactly the t-interval. For a mean, that's the long way round. The payoff is everything else.

Take a hundred and twenty incomes, skewed enough that the median is the honest summary. Run the same loop, and change one word: median, instead of mean. The medians pile up a little lumpy, because a median can only land near values you actually saw. Their middle ninety-five percent runs from about thirty thousand eight hundred to thirty-seven thousand one hundred. No formula needed.

But the bootstrap can't create information. It only reuses the data you have. Resample a biased sample, and every resample carries the bias: a confident interval... around the wrong center. And it fails at the edges. A resample can never beat the largest value you saw, so it can't say much about a maximum. It measures how much an estimate wobbles, not whether it's aimed at the truth. So an interval says which values are plausible. A test asks about one value in particular... could the effect be zero?
